blind_spots.blind_spot: Hydrogen logistics do not exist at the austere sites their defense pitch names
blind_spots.operator_reality: DoD runs a single-fuel-forward battlefield: JP-8 comes in on every convoy, hydrogen comes in on none. A fuel cell for 'remote bases' or a forward-deployed UAV needs a hydrogen generation/storage/resupply chain the theater doesn't have — the sergeant can top off a diesel generator, not a 700-bar hydrogen cylinder. Same failure mode as the 30fps crowd-detection case: the enabling assumption (fuel availability) is denied by the environment, not the tech.
blind_spots.why_likely_missing: Founder and CTO are PhD materials scientists from a DOE/Argonne commercialization track; their whole framing is DOE cost-per-kg and decarbonization economics, where hydrogen supply is someone else's solved problem.
blind_spots.evidence_quote: long range silent unmanned aerial vehicles, persistent energy storage for satellites and remote bases

blind_spots.blind_spot: Durability is proven against DOE cycle targets, not the environmental qualification that decides an Army or Navy fielding
blind_spots.operator_reality: A membrane that hits a 30,000-cycle bench target still dies in theater from what the bench never sees: sand and dust ingestion into the stack's air side, -30C cold starts, vibration on a ground support vehicle, shock qual for anything sub-safe. MIL-STD-810 environmental results and platform-level qual data — not DOE ultimate targets — are what the transition decision reads, and their language never mentions them.
blind_spots.why_likely_missing: Their customers to date are DOE programs and commercial fuel-cell integrators, so every credibility metric they publish is a civilian benchmark; nobody on the 13-person team has had to assemble a military qualification package.
blind_spots.evidence_quote: 5x fuel cell durability. Hits the DOE 30,000-cycle ultimate target ahead of schedule.

blind_spots.blind_spot: 'Drop-in ready' component with no visible path through the prime/platform integration chain
blind_spots.operator_reality: A membrane reaches a Navy submarine or an Army vehicle only inside someone else's stack, inside a prime's platform, inside a program office's schedule — subcontract flow-downs, GFE interfaces, airworthiness or sub-safe certification measured in years. Claiming the same part serves a submarine oxygen generator and a data center skips the part where the defense variant needs its own multi-year qualification lineage; 'drop-in' for a commercial electrolyzer is not drop-in for a program of record.
blind_spots.why_likely_missing: As a materials supplier two tiers below the platform, they see the membrane spec, not the acquisition mechanics above it; no prime partner or qualification program is named anywhere on the site.
blind_spots.evidence_quote: The same membrane that goes into a Navy submarine oxygen generator goes into a fuel cell for truck, ship, and data center power.

opener_hook: Celadyne's Army SBIR Phase II started October 2024 with roughly 13 people, and every durability number on celadynetech.com is a DOE target — not one is the MIL-STD-810 or fuel-logistics number an Army fielding decision actually reads.
what_they_do: Materials startup making next-generation proton exchange membranes (Dura, Electra) that make hydrogen fuel cells more durable and electrolyzers more efficient, selling into defense (Army/AF SBIRs, submarine oxygen generation claims) and industrial decarbonization markets.
